blocks.text: 1. Layers
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444649765-583767664.png

Neurons, the previous topic, covered one single computational unit in full mechanical detail. A layer is simply many of those individual neurons, computed together, side by side, all sharing the exact same input.

Every network covered throughout this entire course is built by stacking layers, one after another, exactly the structure already introduced conceptually in the What Is Deep Learning and Multi-Layer Perceptron topics, now covered here in full technical depth.
2. The Anatomy of a Layer
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444649765-389049035.png

A layer receives the exact same input, whether that input comes from the raw data or from the previous layer's own output. Every neuron within that layer then processes that same shared input independently of every other neuron in the same layer.

Each neuron applies its own separate, individually learned weights and bias to that shared input, exactly the anatomy already covered in the Neurons topic. The layer's overall output is simply the collection of every individual neuron's own separate output, gathered together into one combined vector.
3. A Layer as One Matrix Operation

blocks.alt: A Layer as One Matrix Operation
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444650476-441054168.png

This connects directly back to the vectorized computation already covered in the Neurons topic. A layer's entire computation, every single neuron within it, gets expressed as one single matrix multiplication in real implementations.

The input vector gets multiplied by a weight matrix, with a bias vector added on top, and the result passes through one shared activation function, producing the entire layer's output in a single, efficient operation rather than computing each neuron separately, one at a time.
4. A Layer's Shape
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444650476-243495605.png

A layer's shape is described by two numbers. Input size describes how many values this layer expects to receive, and this number must exactly match the previous layer's own output size, or the computation simply cannot proceed.

Output size describes how many neurons this layer actually contains, and this number becomes the input size for whichever layer comes directly next in the network. Getting these two numbers to line up correctly across an entire network is a genuinely essential, foundational part of building one correctly.

blocks.text: 5. The Stacking Chain
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444650477-330169809.png

Stacking layers together requires their shapes to chain correctly. Layer 1's output size must exactly equal Layer 2's input size, and Layer 2's own output size must, in turn, exactly equal Layer 3's input size, continuing this exact chain across however many layers a network actually has.

A mismatch anywhere in this chain, a layer expecting an input size that the previous layer does not actually produce, causes a network to fail outright before it can even run, a genuinely common, easily fixed error covered in more practical depth in the Training Deep Networks module later in this course.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A shape mismatch between two stacked layers is one of the most common errors when first building a network by hand, and it is always worth double-checking a layer's declared input size against the actual output size of whatever feeds into it.

blocks.text: 6. Three Roles a Layer Can Play

blocks.alt: Three Roles a Layer Can Play
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444650478-136044655.png

A layer can play one of three roles within a network. The input layer, covered in its own dedicated topic immediately next, receives the raw features and performs no actual computation of its own, simply passing that raw data onward.

The hidden layer, covered right after that, transforms its input into a new, learned representation, and the output layer, covered right after that, produces the network's actual final prediction. Every network in this course is built from exactly these three roles, in exactly this order.

blocks.text: 7. Parameters Per Layer

This connects back to the per-neuron parameter counting already covered in the Neurons topic. A layer's total weight parameters equal its input size multiplied by its output size, since every single neuron in the layer connects to every single value in the input.

Plus exactly one bias per neuron in that layer, added on top of the weight count. This calculation is exactly how a network's total parameter count, a number often cited when comparing different network sizes, actually gets computed layer by layer.
8. A Shared Activation Function

A genuinely common, though not universal, convention is that every neuron within one single layer typically uses the same activation function, covered in full depth in the very next module, Activation Functions, immediately following this one.

Different layers within the same network can use genuinely different activation functions from each other, though, one function commonly used for hidden layers, and a different, often specifically chosen function used for the output layer, depending on exactly what kind of prediction that output layer needs to produce.
9. Why Organizing Neurons Into Layers Matters

blocks.alt: Why Organizing Neurons Into Layers Matters
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444650478-508901471.png

Organizing neurons into layers, rather than treating a network as one giant, unstructured collection of individual units, genuinely matters because it enables the exact matrix multiplication already covered earlier in this topic.

This layered structure is precisely what modern Deep Learning frameworks, and the GPUs they run on, are specifically built to optimize, exactly the compute ingredient already covered in the Why Deep Learning Works topic. Without this organized, layered structure, training a network at any real scale would be considerably less practical.
10. Worked Example
The example below builds a single layer directly from its weight matrix and bias vector, then verifies its shape chains correctly with a second stacked layer.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def relu(x):
    return np.maximum(0, x)

class Layer:
    def __init__(self, input_size, output_size):
        self.weights = np.random.RandomState(42).normal(scale=0.5, size=(input_size, output_size))
        self.biases = np.zeros(output_size)
        self.input_size = input_size
        self.output_size = output_size

    def forward(self, x):
        return relu(x @ self.weights + self.biases)

layer1 = Layer(input_size=4, output_size=8)   # 4 features in, 8 neurons
layer2 = Layer(input_size=8, output_size=3)   # must match layer1's output size

assert layer1.output_size == layer2.input_size, "Shape mismatch between stacked layers"

sample_input = np.array([1.0, -0.5, 2.0, 0.3])
layer1_output = layer1.forward(sample_input)
layer2_output = layer2.forward(layer1_output)

print(f"Layer 1 output shape: {layer1_output.shape}, values: {layer1_output}")
print(f"Layer 2 output shape: {layer2_output.shape}, values: {layer2_output}")
print(f"\nLayer 1 parameters: {layer1.weights.size + layer1.biases.size}")
print(f"Layer 2 parameters: {layer2.weights.size + layer2.biases.size}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The assert statement in this example directly checks the stacking chain covered earlier in this topic, catching a shape mismatch immediately rather than letting it fail confusingly later during the actual forward pass.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A layer is many neurons computed together, side by side, sharing the exact same input.
A layer's entire computation is one matrix multiplication: input times weight matrix, plus bias, through one activation.
A layer's shape is its input size, matching the previous layer's output, and its output size, its own neuron count.
Each layer's output size must exactly equal the next layer's input size, forming an unbroken chain across a network.
A layer can play one of three roles: input, hidden, or output.
A layer's total parameters equal input size times output size for weights, plus one bias per neuron.
Neurons within a layer typically share an activation function, though different layers can use different ones.
Organizing neurons into layers enables the efficient matrix multiplication modern frameworks and GPUs are built to optimize.
